chunks: "I'd group them into three buckets. The biggest is switching . An NFET as a low-side switch lets a 3. 3 volts microcontroller pin turn a motor, solenoid or LED strip on and off.
PFETs are used as high-side load switches to cut power to a subsystem.

In power electronics, MOSFETs are the switches in buck and boost converters and H-bridges for motors, and they replace diodes in synchronous rectifiers and ideal-diode circuits because a few milliohms beats a 0.
4 volts diode drop. There are also protection uses, like a PFET for reverse-battery protection or two FETs back-to-back in a battery pack. The second is digital logic .
Every CMOS gate, processor and memory is built from NMOS and PMOS pairs, and DRAM and flash cells are MOSFET-based too. The third is analog .
In saturation a MOSFET is a voltage-controlled current source, so you get amplifiers, current mirrors, and the pass element in an LDO.
In triode it's a voltage-controlled resistor, which is how analog switches, multiplexers and sample-and-holds work.
And a single NFET with pull-ups makes a bidirectional I²C level shifter.
The reason it's everywhere is the insulated gate: no DC drive current, easy to drive from logic, and very low on-resistance."
